1.meaning: A command meaning "Say!" or "Declare!" — Allah is instructing the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to proclaim aloud the declaration that follows. It frames the whole surah as a divine message to be spoken to people, not the Prophet's own words.
1.grammar: Command verb (imperative), addressed to a single male — "you, say!" It comes from the verb qāla ("to say"). In the command form the middle weak letter (wāw) drops out, leaving a short, sharp qul that ends in a silent (sukūn) lām — exactly how a direct order to one person is formed.

2.meaning: "He" — a standalone pronoun pointing to Allah. Placed first for emphasis, it serves as the subject of the sentence: "He [is]…," setting up the declaration of who Allah is.
2.grammar: Detached subject pronoun, third-person masculine singular ("He"). Arabic has no separate word for "is," so "He" + "Allah" together already mean "He is Allah." Its fixed final -a (huwa) is part of the word itself, not a case ending, since pronouns do not change for case.

3.meaning: "Allah" — the unique personal name of the one true God, the Necessary Being who possesses every perfection and is free of every flaw. Here it functions as the predicate: "He is Allah."
3.grammar: Proper name (the divine name). The al- at the front is part of the name itself. The final -u (…hu) is the nominative (raf') ending: it marks Allah as the predicate identifying "He," i.e. "He is Allah." The transliteration "l-lahu" shows the opening vowel dropped after the previous word, which is normal in connected recitation.
3.root: — (proper name; traditionally linked to the idea of the one worthy of worship, but treated as a name, not a derived word)

4.meaning: "One" in the deepest sense: utterly single and unique — not one of a series, not one part of a pair, and not made of parts. It affirms that Allah is absolutely indivisible and that nothing resembles or shares in His being.
4.grammar: Noun/adjective acting as a second predicate — "[He is] One." The ending -un (aḥadun) is the nominative case combined with tanwīn (the doubled "n" sound) that marks it as indefinite — "One," not "the one" — underscoring His absolute, unshared oneness. The case matches "He is Allah," stacking a second statement: "He is Allah; He is One."

1.meaning: Allah — the proper, personal name of the One True God in Arabic. It is not a common noun like 'a god' or 'the deity'; it names the single, unique Being who alone is worthy of worship, perfect in every attribute and free of every flaw. Here it opens the verse as the subject: 'Allah is...'

parts.en: the (definite article, fused into the name)

1.grammar: This is the subject of the sentence, and the verse is a pure equational sentence with no verb ('Allah [is] the Self-Sufficient'). The final -u ending is the nominative case, which is the marker Arabic puts on the subject — the one the statement is about. The al- at the front is the definite article 'the', here permanently bonded into the Name itself.
1.root: Linguistically connected to ʾ-l-h (relating to worship/divinity), but as the unique proper Name of God it is treated as having no ordinary derivable root — —

2.meaning: al-Samad — a single dense Arabic word with no clean English equivalent, here describing Allah. It carries two linked ideas at once: (1) the absolutely Self-Sufficient One who needs nothing and no one; and (2) the One upon whom every created thing utterly depends, the supreme Master to whom all turn for every need. He is the eternal, undiminishing refuge that all creation leans on while He leans on nothing. Renderings like 'the Eternal', 'the Absolute', or 'the Sustainer needed by all' each capture only part of it.

parts.en: the Self-Sufficient One on whom all depend

2.grammar: This word is the predicate — it tells us what Allah is. Its final -u ending is the nominative case, matching the subject 'Allah' (both subject and predicate of an equational sentence take this ending). The al- ('the') makes it definite and exclusive: not merely 'a self-sufficient one' but THE Self-Sufficient, the only one truly deserving the title. Note that ص is a 'sun letter': the 'l' of al- assimilates into the following 'ṣ' sound, so although it is written al- + ṣamad, in the full word الصَّمَدُ this assimilation produces a doubled ṣ (shaddah) at the junction and it is pronounced 'aṣ-ṣamad'. The base word itself is صَمَد, with no inherent shaddah.
2.root: ص-م-د (ṣ-m-d) — to turn to / resort to (someone in authority); hence the One sought out by all, who is Himself in need of none

1.meaning: A negative particle meaning "not / did not." It is special because it takes a present-tense verb but pushes its meaning firmly into the past, giving an absolute, settled denial: "He has never, at any point, done this." Here it sets up the declaration that Allah has never fathered any offspring.
1.grammar: A particle of negation (called a "jussive" particle) that governs the verb after it: it changes a present-tense verb into a negated past meaning and clips its ending to a bare, vowel-less form. So although the next word looks present-tense, "lam" makes it mean "He did not / has never."

2.meaning: "He fathers / begets" — to produce a child, to have offspring. Under the negation "lam" the sense becomes "He has never fathered anyone," denying that Allah has any son or child whatsoever.
2.grammar: A present-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular: the "ya-" prefix marks "he." The root is و-ل-د, but in the active form the first root-letter waw drops out (a regular feature of waw-initial verbs), leaving just "-lid." Because the particle "lam" governs it, the verb is in the clipped (jussive) form — its ending loses its vowel and shows a silent stop (yalid, not yalidu). That clipped ending is exactly what signals it is being negated as a past fact: "He has never begotten."
2.root: و-ل-د (w-l-d) — to give birth, beget, offspring

3.meaning: "And not" — the connector "and" joined to the same negative particle "lam." It links a second denial to the first: not only has Allah never fathered anyone, but in addition He Himself was never born.
3.grammar: Two pieces joined: the prefix "wa-" means "and," and "lam" is again the negation particle that puts the following verb into the negated-past, clipped (jussive) form. Together they add a parallel second negation to the verse.

4.meaning: "He was born / He was fathered." Under the negation this denies that Allah came into being from a parent or origin: He was never born, never begotten, never brought into existence by anything. He is eternal and uncaused.
4.grammar: A present-tense verb in the PASSIVE voice, 3rd-person masculine singular — "he is born / begotten" (something done TO him), not "he gives birth." The passive is shown by the vowel pattern: a "u" on the "yu-" prefix and a fatha ("a") on the last stem-letter (yūlad rather than the active yalid). Note the middle "ū": it is the first root-letter waw of و-ل-د, NOT a passive marker. In the active form (yalid) that waw drops out, but the passive vowel pattern keeps it in place, where it surfaces as a long "ū." Governed by "lam," the verb takes the clipped (jussive) ending — silent, vowel-less — giving the negated past sense: "He was never born."
4.root: و-ل-د (w-l-d) — to give birth, beget, offspring

1.meaning: "And not..." — the opening links this verse to the ones before it ("and"), then begins a firm denial. The little word lam is a negator with a special job: it pushes the verb that follows it into the past and denies it ever happened. So the sense building here is "and there has never been...".
1.grammar: Two pieces joined. wa- is the connector "and." lam is a negative particle that does two things at once: it flips a present-tense verb into a denied past ("did not / has never"), and it is jussive (jazm), meaning it strips the ending off the following verb down to a bare sukūn (no vowel). It always sits directly before its verb.
1.root: — (particles: wa = "and," lam = negation; no triliteral root)

2.meaning: "...there has been / there existed..." From the verb kāna, "to be / to exist." Paired with lam before it, the meaning becomes "there has never been" — a denial that something has ever existed at any point. It is impersonal here, setting up "there has never been [anyone]...".
2.grammar: An imperfect (present-tense) verb, 3rd-person masculine singular, "he/it is," built from the prefix ya- ("he/it") on the stem of kāna. Two things shape its form: (1) lam before it makes it mean a denied past — "has not been"; (2) because lam is jussive, the normal indicative ending -u is dropped, leaving the final consonant with a bare sukūn — that is why it is yakun, not yakūnu. The shortened ending (-n with no vowel) is the visible mark of lam's jussive grip on it.
2.root: ك-و-ن (k-w-n) — being, existing, coming to be

3.meaning: "...for Him / belonging to Him." A small two-part word meaning roughly "to Him" or "His." In the flow of the verse it carries the idea "there has never been, belonging to Him, any equal" — i.e., He has never had anyone equal to Him.
3.grammar: A preposition plus an attached pronoun. The preposition is li- ("to / for / belonging to"); when an attached pronoun follows, li- regularly shifts its vowel to la- before the pronoun -hu, giving the surface form lahu (recited with a slight lengthening, lahū). -hu is the attached pronoun "Him," referring to Allah. Grammatically this phrase "for Him" fills the predicate (khabar) slot of kāna — "there has never been, for Him, [an equal]" — and signals possession: Allah having (or rather never having) an equal.

4.meaning: "...equal, comparable, a match." A kufuw is a peer — someone or something on the same level, an equivalent or counterpart. The verse denies that any such match to Allah has ever existed: nothing is His equal, His like, or His rival.
4.grammar: A noun, "an equal." The ending is -an (written as tanwīn fatḥ, the double-fatḥa on the final alif), which marks two things at once: the doubled-n sound (tanwīn) means it is indefinite — "an equal," not "the equal"; and the -a vowel is the accusative case (manṣūb), which flags it as the predicate (khabar) of kāna. It is brought forward ahead of its subject for emphasis, so the stress falls on "equal" — "there has never been [as] an equal to Him anyone."
4.root: ك-ف-ء (k-f-ʾ) — being equal, matching, being a counterpart

5.meaning: "...anyone / a single one." aḥad means "one" in the sense of "any one at all." After a negation like this, it sweeps the field completely: not even one — no one whatsoever — has ever been equal to Him. It echoes aḥad ("One") in verse 1, framing the whole sūrah: He is One, and no one is His match.
5.grammar: A noun, "anyone." The ending is -un (tanwīn ḍamm, the double-ḍamma). The doubled-n (tanwīn) marks it as indefinite — "any one"; the -u vowel is the nominative case (marfūʿ), which identifies it as the subject (ism) of yakun ("there has [never] been"). The subject is held back to the very end of the verse, landing the final emphasis on "anyone." Coming after the negation, aḥad means "not a single one."
5.root: ء-ح-د (ʾ-ḥ-d) — oneness, unity, a single one
